The Itinerary

Sunday, May 10
Arrival Day
NH 125 lands ~9 PM · Keikyu to hotel · Konbini dinner
▾
NH 125 arrives Haneda Terminal 2 ~9 PM JST. You'll be through customs by 10 PM. Priority: buy Suica before you do anything else. The vending machine is left of the Tokyo Monorail gate in the arrivals hall.
~10 PM
Get your Suica cards 📍 Haneda T2 arrivals hall
At the Tokyo Monorail entrance in T2 arrivals, use the Welcome Suica vending machine. Load ¥5,000 (~$35) each. This is your wallet, transit card, and convenience store payment for the whole week. iPhone users: add Suica directly to Apple Wallet at the airport Suica vending machine or in advance via the app.
⚡ Do this first
Welcome Suica info
~10:30 PM
Keikyu Airport Line to hotel 🚆 Train · ~40 min from T2
From Haneda T2: take the Keikyu Airport Line toward Asakusa (Toei Asakusa Line). Exit at Ueno-Okachimachi or Ueno Station. Short walk to your apartment. ~40 min, ~¥600 (~$4)/person. Tap your Suica. No taxi needed tonight — this line runs until midnight.
Keikyu → Toei Asakusa Line~¥600 (~$4) pp
Late
Konbini dinner + crash 🚶 Walk · 2 min from hotel
Do not try to find a restaurant tonight. Go to the nearest Lawson or 7-Eleven (every corner in Ueno). Japanese convenience store food is genuinely excellent — fresh onigiri, katsu sandwiches, hot ramen, steamed buns. Grab Pocari Sweat to hydrate after the flight. Jet lag will wake you at 4–5 AM — that's actually perfect for tomorrow.
¥500–800 (~$3.50–5.50) ppSleep — tomorrow starts at dawn
1
Monday, May 11
Tokyo: Fish Market + Old Streets
Toyosu at dawn · Yanaka · Ameyoko · Hoppy Street night
▾
Jet lag works in your favor today. You'll be awake at 4–5 AM. Use it — Toyosu opens at 5 AM and is utterly magical at dawn when only market workers are there. The tuna auction runs 5:30–6:30 AM.
5:00 AM
Toyosu Fish Market — tuna auction 🚆 Train · ~35 min from hotel (Hibiya Line + Yurikamome)
From Ueno, take the Hibiya Line to Tsukiji, walk to Shimbashi, then ride the Yurikamome monorail to Shijo-mae Station (right at the market entrance). Enter the Fisheries Wholesale Market Building by 5:30 AM to watch the tuna auction from the observation gallery — massive frozen bluefins sold in a frenzy of hand signals. Free, no lottery needed for the gallery.
Hibiya Line + YurikamomeFree entry
Toyosu Market official site
7:00 AM
Sushi breakfast — Sushi Dai 🚶 Walk · 2 min (3rd floor, same building)
Head to Toyosu Gurume (3rd floor, Intermediate Wholesale Building). Go to Sushi Dai — expect a line but it moves fast. The 12-piece omakase set is ~¥4,000 (~$28). This is the freshest sushi on earth, made with fish bought at auction 30 minutes earlier. Worth every yen and every minute of the queue.
~¥4,000 (~$28) ppArrive before 7:30 or queue gets long
Find on Google Maps
9:30 AM
Tsukiji Outer Market — old market streets 🚶 Walk or 🚆 train · 3 km / ~15 min walk, or Yurikamome + 5 min walk
After Toyosu, make your way to Tsukiji (3 km walk across bridges, or quick Yurikamome + walk). The outer market still buzzes: fishmongers, knife shops, tamagoyaki egg-roll stalls, dashi shops. Buy a takeaway sea urchin cup, browse the handmade knife shops. Avoid the tourist shops on the main drag — go one row deeper.
Free to browseBring cash — many stalls cash only
Tsukiji Outer Market
11:30 AM
Yanaka — old Tokyo neighborhood 🚆 Train · ~20 min (Hibiya Line to Nippori)
Ride Metro to Nippori Station. Yanaka is Tokyo's best-preserved Shitamachi (old downtown) — narrow lanes, wooden houses, a cemetery locals use as a park. Walk Yanaka Ginza shopping street (50s-era storefronts). Buy taiyaki (fish-shaped sweet cakes). Poke into craft shops. This is where old Tokyo still lives.
Nippori Station exitFree
Yanaka — Tokyo Tourism Guide
2:00 PM
Ameyoko market + afternoon rest 🚆 Train · ~5 min (JR to Ueno) or 15 min walk
Walk back via Ameyoko — the outdoor market running under JR tracks between Ueno and Okachimachi. Dried seafood, cheap produce, Korean food stalls, army surplus. Loud, chaotic, 100% local. Two minutes from your apartment. Then: nap. You've been awake for 30+ hours.
2 min from your apartment
7:00 PM
Standing sushi near Okachimachi 🚆 Train · ~5 min (JR to Akihabara)
Uogashi Nihon-ichi chain has a branch near Akihabara — nigiri from ¥80 (~$0.55) a piece, super fresh seasonal fish, where office workers eat standing up at a counter. This is not a tourist experience. This is Monday evening in Tokyo.
~¥1,500 (~$10) pp
Find Uogashi on Google Maps
8:30 PM
Hoppy Street, Asakusa — local night 🚆 Train · ~8 min (Ginza Line to Asakusa)
One Metro stop to Asakusa. Walk to Hoppy Street (ホッピー通り) — a string of old izakayas with plastic outdoor tables, paper lanterns, yakitori smoke, and Hoppy (a local low-alcohol beer substitute that's been a Tokyo staple since 1948). Communal tables, strangers becoming friends. Order: Hoppy, chicken gizzards, grilled leek, edamame. Zero tourists. All local.
Asakusa area¥1,500–2,000 (~$10–14) pp

Tuesday, May 12
Tokyo: Skytree + Expat Neighborhoods + Sento
Ueno lake walk · Tokyo Skytree top · Shimokitazawa · Nakameguro · Ebisu Yokocho
▾
7:30 AM
Morning walk — Ueno Park & Shinobazu Pond
Start the day with a walk through Ueno Park along Shinobazu Pond (不忍池) — a large lotus lake right on your doorstep. In May the lotus leaves are spreading across the surface and the waterside path is calm and unhurried. Vendors are just setting up, elderly locals are doing tai chi, and the whole park feels like it belongs to the city rather than tourists. A peaceful 45-minute loop before the day gets busy.
5 min from apartmentFree
9:00 AM
Tokyo Skytree — to the top ⭐ 🚆 Train · ~10 min (Ginza Line Ueno → Asakusa, 2 stops, then walk 10 min)
At 634 metres, Tokyo Skytree is the tallest tower in the world and an unmissable experience. Buy tickets to the Tembo Deck (350m) — on a clear May morning the views across the entire Kanto plain are extraordinary. You can see Mt. Fuji on clear days. Add the Tembo Galleria (450m) if you want the very top — a spiralling glass walkway. The structure itself is a feat of engineering worth understanding.

Book tickets online in advance — queues without pre-booking can be 60–90 minutes. Online booking is the same price and gets you straight in.
Tembo Deck ¥2,100 (~$14) · +Galleria ¥1,000 (~$7)⭐ Must-see — book online
Tokyo Skytree — book tickets
12:00 PM
Shimokitazawa — bohemian Tokyo 🚆 Train · ~35 min (Ginza Line to Shibuya, Keio Inokashira to Shimokitazawa)
Head from Asakusa to Shimokitazawa. This is where young Tokyoites actually live: vintage clothing shops, tiny independent cafes, live music venues, zero chain stores, zero tourists. Wander without a plan. Stop at Bear Pond Espresso for coffee (tiny, serious, third-wave). Browse a vintage shop like Flamingo. Just observe the city being itself.
Keio Inokashira from ShibuyaBrowse free
Shimokitazawa guide (Time Out)
1:30 PM
Lunch: ramen or curry in Shimokitazawa 📍 Same area · no transit needed
Find a ramen shop on a back street — look for a handwritten sign and a queue of 3–5 people. Or a small Japanese curry shop where the lunch set is ¥850 (~$6) and a salaryman is eating alone at the counter next to you. This is what everyday Tokyo tastes like.
¥800–1,200 (~$5.50–8.25) pp
3:00 PM
Cat Street, Harajuku — the anti-tourist shopping street 🚆 Train · ~10 min (Odakyu to Harajuku, 5 min walk)
Ride to Harajuku Station, then walk 5 minutes to Cat Street (キャットストリート) — an informal pedestrian lane running parallel to the flashy Omotesando boulevard, but completely different in character. Independent vintage shops, tiny select boutiques, concept stores, street food carts, and cafés you won't find anywhere else. Relaxed and unhurried for central Tokyo. Browse Beams or United Arrows side alleys, duck into a vintage shop, pick up a coffee.
5 min from Harajuku StationFree to browse
Cat Street on Google Maps
5:00 PM
Nakameguro canal walk 🚆 Train · ~10 min (walk to Harajuku → Yamanote to Shibuya → Tokyu 1 stop)
Ride to Nakameguro Station (Tokyu Toyoko Line from Shibuya, one stop). Walk along the Meguro River canal — lined with cherry trees (lush green in May), independent cafes, fashion boutiques, tiny bars. The neighborhood of Tokyo that expats and fashionable locals love. Continue toward Daikanyama — check out Daikanyama T-Site bookstore complex for a glimpse of refined Japanese taste.
Tokyu Toyoko Line from ShibuyaFree
Daikanyama T-Site (English)
7:30 PM
Ebisu Yokocho — hidden izakaya alley 🚶 Walk · ~15 min from Daikanyama or 1 stop on Tokyu
Walk to Ebisu Station. Ebisu Yokocho is a narrow covered alley hidden just behind the station, packed with tiny izakayas — each fits 8 people, communal seating, yakitori, sake, beer. Where local Tokyoites eat on a Tuesday night. Loud, friendly, completely authentic. Order from the handwritten menu or point at what your neighbor is eating.
2 min from Ebisu Station¥2,500–3,500 (~$17–24) pp

Wednesday, May 13
Kyoto Day Trip
Shinkansen at dawn · Fushimi Inari gates early · Nishiki browse · real lunch nearby · Gion old town
▾
Rule for Kyoto: go early, move fast, come back in the evening. Everything key is reachable on foot or a short train ride. Get seat E on the right side to see Mt. Fuji about 40 minutes after departure.
6:30 AM
Shinkansen from Tokyo Station 🚆 Train · ~10 min hotel → Tokyo Station, then 2h 20m to Kyoto
From Ueno, Yamanote Line to Tokyo Station (10 min). Board the Nozomi Shinkansen to Kyoto — first trains ~6 AM, arrives Kyoto ~8:30 AM. Buy a bento box at the station food halls before boarding — eating a bento on a bullet train is a genuine ritual.

Booking tips: If booking last minute and reserved seats are full or complicated, go for the unreserved seats wagon (自由席) — you have a significantly better chance of finding seats together than scrambling for scattered reserved spots. If budget allows, Gran Class or Green Car (business) is an incredibly luxurious experience — wide leather seats, meal service, silence. Worth it once.
Nozomi ~2h 20m¥13,320 (~$92) pp one wayLast minute? → unreserved wagon
JR East — Reserve Shinkansen
9:00 AM
Fushimi Inari — the red gates ⛩️ 🚆 Train · 5 min (JR Nara Line to Inari Station, shrine is at exit)
JR Nara Line from Kyoto Station to Inari Station (5 min, ¥150). Arrive as early as possible — this is the most important rule here. By 10 AM it fills up fast and the tunnel of torii gates becomes a slow-moving tourist parade. Early morning you get the atmosphere it deserves: incense, quiet, the gates glowing orange-red in the low light.

Yes, it's extremely touristy — but it's touristy because it's genuinely extraordinary. Walk the lower gates, then push past the first two stations up the mountain where nearly everyone turns back. Up there it becomes a quiet trail with mossy stone foxes and almost no one around.
⚑ Arrive as early as possibleFreeWear walking shoes
Fushimi Inari official (English)
11:00 AM
Nishiki Market — look, don't eat 🚆 Train · ~15 min (JR back to Kyoto Station, subway to Karasuma-Oike)
Subway to Karasuma-Oike, then walk to Nishiki Market — a 400-year-old covered market street. Visually it's great fun: colourful stalls, pickles stacked high, vendors calling out, everything squeezed into a narrow arcade. Worth a wander and a look around.

Do not eat lunch here. The food stalls are aimed squarely at tourists — overpriced, nothing special, and you'll eat better two minutes away. Browse, soak in the atmosphere, pick up some pickles to take back, then head out for proper food nearby. Keep an eye out for yellow custard mochi — if you spot it, it's a must-try.
Free entry👁 Browse only — eat elsewhere🟡 Yellow custard mochi if you see it
Nishiki Market (English)
12:30 PM
Lunch: step outside Nishiki 🚶 Walk · 2–5 min from the market exits
Step off Nishiki onto any of the side streets heading north or south and look for a small restaurant — calmer, cleaner, and immediately better than anything inside the market. A teishoku set lunch (grilled fish or tofu, miso soup, rice, pickles) from a place with a plastic food display in the window is the move. Kyoto cuisine is lighter and more delicate than Tokyo's. ¥900–1,400 will get you a proper meal.
¥900–1,400 (~$6–10) ppSide streets off Nishiki, not inside it
2:00 PM
Gion old town — backstreets + hidden bar 🚶 Walk · ~15 min east from Nishiki
Skip the main Hanamikoji Street (tourist wall-to-wall). Head east toward the Shirakawa Canal — a narrow waterway lined with old machiya townhouses, stone lanterns, and willow trees. One of the most beautiful and peaceful corners of Kyoto. Continue to Shimbashi Street nearby. Geiko and maiko still use these streets in the afternoon — walk quietly.

From the canal, head to Premium Matcha & Bar Kashoan — Classic Tea & Cocktails: a hidden modern bar tucked inside the old town, serving both matcha-based drinks and cocktails. A genuinely special spot that feels completely out of place with its surroundings — in a good way. Perfect contrast to the ancient streetscape just outside.

📍 〒605-0087 Kyoto, Higashiyama Ward, Motoyoshicho, 46
Free · Shirakawa CanalQuiet hours 2–4 PM best🍵🍸 Kashoan — matcha & cocktails
Open in Google Maps Gion — Kyoto Tourism (English)
5:30 PM
Shinkansen back to Tokyo 🚆 Train · ~15 min to Kyoto Station, then 2h 20m Nozomi to Tokyo
Board the Nozomi back from Kyoto Station, arriving Tokyo ~7:50 PM. Total day cost per person including transport: ~¥30,000 (~$207). Dinner back in Ueno — try a bowl of tonkotsu ramen at Ichiran near Ueno: order at a vending machine, eat alone in a wooden booth, deeply satisfying.
Reserve return seat in advanceRamen ¥1,000–1,200 (~$7–8.30)
Ichiran Ramen

Thursday, May 14
Shopping Day
Starbucks flagship · Don Quijote · Onitsuka Tiger · Omotesando Hills · Kura Sushi
▾
What actually happened — a great shopping day. The route ended up compact and walkable: Starbucks flagship to kick off, then Don Quijote next door, Onitsuka Tiger shoes, Omotesando Hills for the architecture, and Kura Sushi to close it out. Tokyu Hands was skipped — not worth the detour.
10:00 AM
Starbucks flagship store — coffee & cakes
Started the day at the Starbucks flagship — about an hour of coffee and cakes before hitting the shops. A good, unhurried way to ease into a full day of walking. The space itself is worth seeing.
~1 hourCoffee & cake ~¥1,500–2,000 pp
11:00 AM
Don Quijote — next door, quick browse 🚶 Walk · right next door
Don Quijote (Don Ki) is right next to the Starbucks — the classic chaotic multi-floor discount store full of snacks, cosmetics, character goods, and Japanese Kit Kats. Only needs about 15 minutes; you can see what it's about without getting sucked in for too long.
~15 min is plentyOpen until 5 AM
Don Quijote store finder
11:30 AM
Onitsuka Tiger — shoe shopping
The Onitsuka Tiger store — expect a line of tourists outside, so factor in wait time. Worth it: full range of styles including Japan-exclusive colorways you won't find elsewhere. The shoes are made in Japan and the quality difference is noticeable. Mexico 66, Ultimate 81, and the Serrano are the popular picks.
Queue expected — touristsShoes ¥15,000–22,000 (~$103–152)
Onitsuka Tiger store locator
1:00 PM
Omotesando Hills — the spiral
Omotesando Hills, designed by architect Tadao Ando, is worth going in just for the architecture — a beautiful continuous spiral ramp winds through the interior. Browse the shops or just walk the spiral and take it in. One of the most distinctive interiors in Tokyo.
Free to enterAlong Omotesando boulevard
Omotesando Hills (English)
3:00 PM
Tokyu Hands — skip it
Went to Tokyu Hands for stationery — not worth it. Disappointing and not interesting enough to justify the time. Skip and move on.
⚠️ Not recommended
6:00 PM
Dinner: Kura Sushi — next to Uniqlo 🚶 Walk · beside the Uniqlo
Kura Sushi next to the Uniqlo — conveyor belt sushi, very cheap, very loud, and an absolute blast. The sushi was genuinely good and the whole experience is fun and chaotic in the best way. A highlight of the day. Plates come around on the belt or you order via tablet; the little capsule machine that dispenses toys when you finish a set of plates is a nice touch.
~¥1,000–2,000 pp (~$7–14)Loud & lively — embrace it
Kura Sushi (English)
8:00 PM
CN Massage — late evening wind-down
Finished the day with a massage at CN Massage. Fine for the price — nothing special, nothing to write home about, and a bit expensive for what it was. Decent enough after a long day on foot but wouldn't prioritise it again.
⚠️ Overpriced for the quality
5
Friday, May 15
Tokyo at Night
Nezu shrine · Shinjuku · Golden Gai · Shibuya at midnight
▾
Your last full night. Start slow, end late. Tokyo's nightlife rewards patience — the best bars are up unmarked staircases in anonymous buildings. The city is completely safe to wander at 2 AM. Last trains are ~midnight; taxi home after or stay until the 5 AM first trains.
10:00 AM
Nezu Shrine + kissaten coffee 🚶 Walk · 15 min from hotel
Nezu Shrine is a 15-minute walk from your apartment — a vermillion torii tunnel like Fushimi Inari but in Tokyo, almost entirely unknown to tourists. The azalea mountain garden behind the main hall is in peak bloom in May. Afterward, find a local kissaten (old-school Japanese coffee shop) near Yushima for a thick cotton drip coffee and morning toast set (buttered toast, boiled egg, coffee ¥700 (~$4.85)). A dying art form. Cherish it.
15 min walk from hotelShrine free · Coffee ¥700 (~$4.85)
Nezu Shrine official (English)
1:00 PM
Akihabara — electric town walk 🚆 Train · ~5 min (1 stop from Okachimachi on JR)
One subway stop to Akihabara. Even if you're not into anime, the raw density of it — multi-floor electronics stores, capsule machines, tiny component shops, maid cafe flyers being handed out — is a genuine Tokyo experience that exists nowhere else. Walk through the back streets, not the main drag. Grab a standing ramen bowl.
1 stop from Okachimachi
Akihabara — Tokyo Tourism Guide
4:00 PM
Omoide Yokocho — Memory Lane, Shinjuku 🚆 Train · ~15 min (JR Sobu Line to Shinjuku, west exit)
Yamanote Line to Shinjuku, west exit. Omoide Yokocho (Memory Lane) is a narrow 50-meter alley of tiny yakitori stalls where smoke fills the air and salarywomen and men drink under the Chuo train tracks. Very known but still genuinely atmospheric at 5 PM. Beer and skewers, standing or perched on a stool, while trains rumble overhead.
¥1,500–2,000 (~$10–14) ppShinjuku west exit
Omoide Yokocho — Time Out guide
7:00 PM
Golden Gai — the best bar neighborhood on earth 🚶 Walk · 5 min (Shinjuku east side)
Golden Gai: six narrow alleys, ~200 bars, each the size of a large closet — fitting 6 to 8 people maximum. Every bar has a theme: film noir, horror movie posters, jazz records, mountaineering gear, kabuki. Some say "no foreigners" but most welcome you if you bow and ask politely. Find one with a vibe you love. Order what the bartender recommends. Cover charge ¥500–1,000 (~$3.45–6.90). Drinks ¥800 (~$5.50). Stay for two bars.
Shinjuku east sideCover ¥500–1,000 (~$3.45–6.90) + drinksAsk permission to enter
Golden Gai — Time Out guide
10:30 PM
Shibuya crossing at midnight 🚆 Train · ~8 min (Yamanote Line Shinjuku → Shibuya)
Yamanote Line to Shibuya. On a Friday night, Shibuya is loud, alive, astonishing. Cross the scramble intersection with everyone else — it genuinely feels like the world is moving simultaneously. Then walk 3 blocks southwest to Udagawacho — independent bars, izakayas, small clubs, no tourists. Find a bar and stay as long as you want. Taxi home ¥1,500–2,000 (~$10–14). Or wait for the 5 AM first trains and watch the city wake up.
Last trains ~midnightTaxi home ¥1,500–2,000 (~$10–14)

Saturday, May 16
Nikko Day Trip
NACO guided adventure · bikes · rafting · station pickup & dropoff · shrines · forest
▾
Why Nikko? Mountainous, forested, culturally dense, and far less visited than Kyoto. Book a guided day with NACO — they pick you up directly at Tobu-Nikko Station, take you through e-bike rides, river rafting, forest trails, and drop you back at the station. One of the most memorable days you can have near Tokyo. Reserve in advance online.
7:00 AM
Tobu Limited Express to Nikko 🚆 Train · ~10 min hotel → Asakusa Station, then 2h to Nikko
From Asakusa Station: Tobu Limited Express "Revaty Kegon" directly to Tobu-Nikko Station. ~2 hours, ~¥2,720 (~$19) per person (reserved seats, book in advance at the Tobu ticket office or online). Arrive Nikko ~9:30 AM. This train is comfortable and scenic through the Kanto plains into the mountains.
Tobu Asakusa → Tobu-Nikko ~2h~¥2,720 (~$19) pp
Tobu Nikko Line (English)
9:00 AM
NACO meets you at the station 📍 Pickup · Tobu-Nikko Station
NAOC is a Nikko-based outdoor adventure company that picks you up directly at Tobu-Nikko Station and organises a full day out. Activities include electric mountain bikes through the cedar forests, river rafting on the Daiya River, forest hikes, and shrine visits — they tailor the day to your group. Drop-off is back at the station in time for your return train. ⚠️ Reservation required in advance — book via their website before your trip.
Station pickup & dropoff includedVaries by activity — check site
NAOC — Official website (English)
10:00 AM
Ride to Kanmangafuchi Abyss 🚲 Bike · ~10 min (2 km from rental shop)
Skip the main shrine first. Ride north to Kanmangafuchi Abyss — a riverside gorge with a row of 70+ moss-covered Jizo statues lining the path alongside rushing water. Eerily quiet, beautiful, and almost never crowded. Lock bikes at the entrance, walk the stone path for 20 minutes. One of the strangest and most moving places near Tokyo.
~2 km ride from rental shopFree
Kanmangafuchi Abyss (English)
11:00 AM
Nikko Toshogu Shrine complex 🚲 Bike · ~10 min uphill (e-assist makes it easy)
Ride up to the World Heritage shrine complex. Lock bikes and walk the cedar-lined avenue. The ¥1,300 (~$9) combined ticket covers Toshogu Shrine and surrounding temples. The gold-lacquered shrines are genuinely spectacular — more ornate than anything you'll see elsewhere in Japan. Take the path behind the Nemuri-Neko (Sleeping Cat) carving up 207 stone steps to Tokugawa Ieyasu's forested tomb.
¥1,300 (~$9) entry
Nikko Toshogu Shrine (English)
1:00 PM
Lunch at a farm 🌾 Farm · arranged through NAOC
A standout meal — lunch at a local farm in the Nikko countryside. Fresh, simple, homegrown food in a setting you won't find in Tokyo. NAOC can arrange this as part of the day. Expect rice, vegetables, and local produce straight from the land. Quiet, unhurried, genuinely great.
Farm-to-table lunch · included or arranged via NAOC
2:30 PM
Forest trail ride + return 🚲 Bike · ~20 min into cedar forest, return to rental by 4:30 PM
Ride further into the cedar forest toward Takino-o Shrine — a small waterfall shrine on a trail through ancient trees that almost no one visits. The e-bikes handle the incline easily. NAOC will bring you back to Tobu-Nikko Station in time to catch the 5 PM Tobu express back to Tokyo.
Forest trailFree
5:00 PM
Return to Tokyo + tonkatsu dinner 🚆 Train · 2h Tobu Express to Asakusa, then 10 min to hotel
Tobu Express back to Asakusa, arrive ~7 PM. Dinner: find a small tonkatsu (breaded pork cutlet) shop near Ueno or Okachimachi. Any standing tonkatsu counter with a handwritten daily set menu is excellent. Meal with rice, miso soup, shredded cabbage: ¥1,200 (~$8.30).
¥1,200 (~$8.30) pp
7
Sunday, May 17 → departs 00:40 Mon
Last Day + Airport
Coin lockers at Ueno Station · Ueno park · Ryogoku · Final dinner · Depart 11 PM
▾
NH 106 departs Haneda at 00:40 Monday May 18 — technically Monday morning but you're going tonight. Leave for the airport at 11 PM — bags are already at Ueno Station coin lockers all day, so there's no apartment detour. From Ueno, take the JR Keihin-Tohoku Line south to Shinagawa (~20 min), then the Keikyu Airport Line directly to Haneda Terminal 2 (~25 min). Total ~45 min, arriving around 11:45 PM. Once through check-in and security, the international terminal has last-minute omiyage shops: matcha Kit Kats, Tokyo Banana, premium sake. Use any remaining Suica balance at the terminal 7-Eleven.
8:00 AM
Store bags at Ueno Station coin lockers 🚶 Walk · 5 min from apartment
Pack before you go to bed on Saturday night. Sunday morning, walk luggage to JR Ueno Station — large coin lockers are available on the ground floor near the Shinobazu and Iriya exits. Large locker fits a suitcase: ¥700–900 (~$5–6) per locker for the day, paid by IC card (Suica works). Store everything here so you spend the entire day completely hands-free. Collect bags when you return from dinner at ~10 PM before heading to the airport. Tip: lockers are first-come-first-served — arrive early to secure a large one. If Ueno is full, Okachimachi Station (2 min walk) also has lockers.
5 min walk¥700–900 (~$5–6) per lockerLarge lockers · Suica accepted
Ueno Station coin lockers — Google Maps
9:00 AM
Ueno Park morning walk 🚶 Walk · 5 min from hotel
Ueno Park is right next to your apartment — on Sunday morning it fills with locals: families, joggers, old men playing shogi, street musicians, food carts. Walk along Shinobazu Pond, watch the lotus flowers on the water, stop at a park-side coffee stall. This is the version of Tokyo you've been living in all week, at its most relaxed.
5 min from apartmentFree
Ueno Park — Tokyo Tourism
11:00 AM
Ryogoku — sumo town lunch 🚆 Train · ~10 min (JR Yamanote to Akihabara, JR Sobu 2 stops to Ryogoku)
Take the JR Sobu Line two stops to Ryogoku — the historic home of sumo in Tokyo. Walk past the Kokugikan sumo arena, browse the sumo shops on the main street, then sit down for chankonabe — the rich, hearty hot pot that sumo wrestlers eat to bulk up. Deeply good, very filling, very local. Ryogoku feels nothing like the rest of Tokyo.
JR Sobu Line 2 stops from AkihabaraChankonabe ¥1,500–2,000 (~$10–14) pp
Ryogoku — Tokyo Tourism
2:00 PM
Last Ameyoko walk 🚆 Train · ~10 min back from Ryogoku (JR Sobu to Akihabara, Yamanote to Ueno)
Head back to the Ueno area for one last slow walk through Ameyoko market — bags are safely in lockers at Ueno Station so you're travelling light. Buy any final snacks, dried seafood, or last-minute souvenirs. Use up remaining Suica balance at the 7-Eleven. No packing stress: everything is already done.
2 min from Ueno Station
5:30 PM
Final dinner — yakitori under the tracks 🚆 Train · ~15 min (Yamanote Line to Yurakucho)
Last meal deserves something special. Head to Yurakucho — under the JR train tracks between Yurakucho and Shimbashi stations there's a legendary row of yakitori restaurants that have been there for decades. Smoky, loud, perfect. Order everything: tsukune meatballs, negima chicken and leek, chicken skin, gizzards, and cold Sapporo. This is how Tokyo locals celebrate. Aim to finish by 9:30 PM to leave time to collect bags from Ueno Station before the airport.
¥3,000–4,000 (~$21–28) pp with drinksYurakucho StationFinish by 9:30 PM

10:00 PM
Collect bags at Ueno Station → Keikyu to Haneda 🚆 Train · ~45 min (JR to Shinagawa + Keikyu Airport Line)
Head from Yurakucho back to Ueno Station (~15 min on Yamanote Line) to retrieve bags from the coin lockers. Then head south: take the JR Keihin-Tohoku Line from Ueno to Shinagawa (~20 min), then switch to the Keikyu Airport Line directly to Haneda Terminal 2 (~25 min). Total journey ~45 min, arriving around 11:45 PM. NH 106 check-in desk closes well before 00:40 — go straight to check-in on arrival. The international terminal has last-minute omiyage shops airside: matcha Kit Kats, Tokyo Banana, premium sake. Use any remaining Suica balance at the terminal 7-Eleven.

Getting Around
Metro · JR · Taxi · Airport train
▾

Your transport toolkit

🚇
Tokyo Metro + Toei Subway — Your daily mode. Tap Suica in and out of every gate. Fares ~¥180–280 (~$1.25–1.95) per ride. Runs until ~midnight.
🚅
JR Yamanote Line — The green loop that circles Tokyo. Covers Shinjuku, Shibuya, Ueno, Akihabara. Also on Suica.
🚕
Taxi — Safe, honest, always metered. ~¥730 (~$5) to start, ~¥1,500–2,000 (~$10–14) for a 10-min ride. Order via GO app. Pay with Suica: say "Suica de" (swee-ka deh) and tap your card or phone. Don't tip — the driver will chase you to return extra change. Always take the receipt — it has the cab's ID number, making lost items nearly 100% recoverable.
✈
Haneda ↔ Hotel — Keikyu Airport Line from T2 toward Asakusa (Toei Asakusa Line), exit Ueno-Okachimachi. ~40 min, ~¥600 (~$4)/person.
📶
Connectivity
T-Mobile · eSIM · Pocket Wi-Fi · Free hotspots
▾

📶 Internet in Japan — what to do

✅
T-Mobile works in Japan — roams on SoftBank, NTT Docomo, and au. Coverage in Tokyo is solid. The problem is speed: most plans throttle to 128–256 Kbps after your high-speed allowance runs out. Fine for Maps and messages, painful for anything else.
📱
Your plan's high-speed allowance — depends on your T-Mobile plan. Go5G Plus/Next: 5 GB then 256 Kbps. Experience Beyond: 15 GB then 256 Kbps. Go5G base: throttled from the start. Check the T-Life app before you leave.
⭐
Easiest solution: Japan eSIM with unlimited data — this is the recommendation. Buy before departure, activate on arrival, done. No hardware, no returns, no throttling. Full local speeds (100–300 Mbps in Tokyo) with truly unlimited data for the whole trip. Each person gets their own — no sharing, no battery anxiety. Holafly Japan eSIM is a reliable option (~$37 pp for 10 days unlimited).
📦
Alternative: Pocket Wi-Fi (airport rental) — a battery-powered hotspot that shares one connection between both phones (~8–12 hrs battery). More hassle than an eSIM — one more device to charge and return by mail at trip end — but works if your phone doesn't support eSIM. Counters are at Haneda T2 arrivals.
📶
Free Wi-Fi top-up: Japan WiFi Auto (NTT) — registers your device once to auto-connect across NTT's free hotspot network at JR stations, airports, convenience stores, and tourist spots. Not a replacement for an eSIM, but a great complement when you're standing in a kombini or riding the Shinkansen. Register here before you go.
💡
Tip: Download Google Maps offline for Tokyo before you leave. Even on a slow connection, offline maps are instant.
💴

Local Rules
Tipping · transit etiquette · cash · dining
▾
  • 1
    Don't tip. Ever. Anywhere. Tipping is considered rude in Japan — it implies the server doesn't earn enough or that you feel superior. Just say gochisousama deshita when you leave (thank you for the meal).
  • 2
    Eat while walking is frowned upon in most places, except at street stalls where it's expected. If you buy something from a stall, eat it right there.
  • 3
    On the subway: be quiet, no phone calls, give up your seat. Nobody talks. Stand on the left of escalators (Tokyo convention) so walkers can pass on the right.
  • 4
    Cash is king at small restaurants, market stalls, and shrines. Always carry ¥5,000–10,000 (~$35–69) on you. Convenience stores and most chain restaurants take cards and Suica.
  • 5
    Standing at the counter at a sushi bar, ramen counter, or tonkatsu joint is completely normal and often results in better food. Don't wait for a table if there are counter seats.
  • 6
    The combini is your friend. Lawson, 7-Eleven, and Family Mart sell genuinely good food, cheap hot coffee, and anything you forgot to pack. The onigiri here is better than sandwiches at most airports anywhere in the world.
  • 7
    At restaurants with no English menu: point confidently at what looks good, say kore (this one), hold up fingers for quantity. Smiling and genuine curiosity go a long way. Most chefs are quietly delighted a foreigner is eating their food.
  • 8
    Umbrella beats rain jacket. Streets are narrow, covered walkways are everywhere, and umbrellas are the overwhelming social norm. Cheap fold-up ones are at every konbini for ¥500–700 (~$3.50–5). Leave the rain jacket packed.
